quick: Threatened miscarriage 5 mg PO three times daily; habitual abortion 5-10 mg daily
May be taken without regard to meals
Used during pregnancy for the licensed indications; avoid in undiagnosed bleeding
Generally avoided; progestogens pass into milk
Continuation of pregnancy, vaginal bleeding, liver function if indicated
summary: Allylestrenol is an orally active synthetic progestogen used in some countries to support pregnancy in threatened and recurrent (habitual) miscarriage and, historically, premature labour. It mimics progesterone, promoting and maintaining a secretory endometrium. It is not FDA-approved; the information here is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF-type sources and regional product labeling.
indications: Prevention of premature labour in selected cases (per regional labeling)

dosage.d: 5 mg three times daily, continued for about 5 to 7 days after symptoms subside; reduce gradually if successful
dosage.t: Continue until symptoms resolve, then taper

dosage.d: 5 to 10 mg daily, started as early as possible and continued through the period of risk
dosage.t: Often continued for one month beyond the gestation at which previous losses occurred

dosage.d: Higher individualized doses per regional labeling, with dose reduction as the situation stabilizes

admin: Administer orally; may be taken with or without food
Start as early as possible in threatened or recurrent miscarriage for best effect
Confirm a viable intrauterine pregnancy and exclude other causes of bleeding before and during use
Taper rather than abruptly stop after successful treatment of threatened miscarriage
Avoid in patients with undiagnosed vaginal bleeding or suspected hormone-dependent malignancy
moa: Allylestrenol is a synthetic derivative structurally related to progesterone. It binds progesterone receptors and exerts progestogenic activity, promoting and maintaining a secretory endometrium, reducing uterine contractility, and supporting the establishment and continuation of pregnancy. It has little or no estrogenic or androgenic activity at therapeutic doses.

absolute: Known or suspected hormone-dependent malignancy (e.g., breast or genital tract)
Active liver disease or history of jaundice in pregnancy
relative: Conditions aggravated by fluid retention (cardiac or renal disease, epilepsy, migraine)

preg: Allylestrenol is intended for use during pregnancy for its licensed indications (threatened and recurrent miscarriage). It should not be used where the pregnancy is nonviable or in undiagnosed bleeding. Use under obstetric supervision; reassure that progestogen support is given to maintain a viable pregnancy.
lact: Progestogens pass into breast milk. Allylestrenol is generally not indicated during breastfeeding and should be avoided unless specifically advised; consider the effect on the infant and milk production.
renal: No specific dose adjustment for renal impairment is established. Use with caution in conditions where fluid retention may be harmful.
hepatic: Avoid in active liver disease or a history of pregnancy-related jaundice. Progestogens are metabolized by the liver, and impaired function may increase exposure.

moderate: Hepatic enzyme inducers (rifampicin, certain anticonvulsants such as phenytoin and carbamazepine) may reduce progestogen levels
Hepatic enzyme inhibitors may increase progestogen levels
minor: May alter the requirements for antidiabetic therapy
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.diagnostics: Progestogens can affect certain endocrine and liver function tests; interpret accordingly

emergency: Signs of a blood clot (leg swelling/pain, chest pain, sudden breathlessness) - seek emergency care
Yellowing of skin or eyes with dark urine (cholestasis) - urgent evaluation

monitoring: Continuation and viability of the pregnancy by clinical and ultrasound assessment
Liver function if jaundice or hepatic symptoms occur
Blood pressure and signs of fluid retention
Glucose control in patients with diabetes
counsel: Take this medicine exactly as prescribed to help support your pregnancy
Do not stop suddenly after a threatened miscarriage settles; your doctor will reduce the dose gradually
Report any heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or leg or chest pain
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, including those for epilepsy or tuberculosis
Keep your antenatal appointments and scans
pk: Progestogenic effect develops over hours to days of dosing
Plasma concentration peaks within a few hours of an oral dose
Supports endometrium with regular daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light and moisture, per product labeling
pearls: Not FDA-approved; information is based on EMA/SmPC and regional product labeling and BNF-type sources
Orally active progesterone-like progestogen used in some countries for threatened and recurrent miscarriage
Confirm a viable pregnancy and exclude other causes of bleeding before use; avoid in nonviable/missed abortion
Taper after successful treatment rather than stopping abruptly
Evidence for progestogen support in miscarriage is debated and practice varies by region
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your usual schedule. Do not take a double dose. Do not stop the medicine on your own.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely to cause serious toxicity; possible effects include nausea, drowsiness, and breast tenderness. Treatment is supportive. Seek advice from a poison control center if a large amount is taken.
